abstract.p: Dark-field scattering imaging and spectroscopy are powerful optical techniques that enable the visualization and analysis of nanoscale materials and optical phenomena with exceptional contrast and sensitivity. They have become indispensable for studying plasmonic nanoparticles, revealing their sizes, shapes, compositions, and optical properties at the single-particle level. This tutorial provides a comprehensive guide for researchers, from the fundamental principles of dark-field scattering to advanced experimental setups, including forward, backward, and evanescent scattering configurations. Practical instructions for performing single-particle scattering imaging and spectroscopy, polarization-dependent measurements, and circular differential scatterometry are presented, with insights into data processing and substrate effects. In addition, we introduce advanced functions such as k-space imaging and hyperspectral dark-field imaging to enrich characterization capabilities. By highlighting the key metrics, emerging applications, and practical considerations, this tutorial is aimed to equip researchers with the knowledge and tools to harness the full potential of dark-field scattering techniques for nanoscale optical studies, ranging from plasmonic systems to quantum nanophotonics.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p:
Dark-field scattering imaging and spectroscopy, techniques that enhance contrast by capturing only scattered light, have been instrumental in uncovering the optical properties of diverse nanoparticles. These techniques have found widespread applications in materials science, nanotechnology, and biomedical research. Their prominence has grown alongside the rise of plasmonics, the discipline investigating interactions between light and metallic nanostructures. Figure illustrates the historical development of dark-field scattering microscopy and plasmonics. The evolution of dark-field scattering microscopy is intricately tied to advancements in optical microscopy, dating back to 1665. Robert Hooke, using self-made single-lens magnifying glasses, conducted microscopic observations. The demand for high-resolution imaging drove innovations in lens technologies, leading to inventions like achromatic lenses, apochromatic lenses, and Abbe condensers. It was not until the late 19th century that efforts to overcome the resolution limits of microscopes gained momentum. Many of such approaches were rooted in the theoretical insights of Hermann von Helmholtz and Ernst Abbe, such as the use of immersion oils with high refractive indices, objectives with high numerical apertures (NAs), and monochromatic objectives for ultraviolet microscopes. These developments culminated in a groundbreaking innovation in 1902 by Richard Adolf Zsigmondy and Henry Siedentopf, who introduced dark-field illumination as a new strategy to enhance the resolution of optical microscopy. They named the first dark-field microscope the “ultramicroscope”, marking a major milestone in the history of microscopy and nanotechnology. The ultramicroscope enabled Zsigmondy to conduct detailed studies of colloids and to visualize individual Au particles as small as 4 nm in solid materials. With the ultramicroscope, Jean Baptiste Perrin was able to track the motion of nanoparticles, and Theodor Svedberg was inspired to invent the ultracentrifuge. By facilitating the in-depth studies of colloids, Zsigmondy’s innovation also laid the foundation for what is now considered the birth of modern nanotechnology. The mid-20th century saw two transformative technologies that revolutionized imaging: the invention of the laser and the charge-coupled device (CCD) cameras, which provided coherent light sources and enabled higher resolution and accuracy in imaging systems. , The 1970s marked further breakthroughs in CCD technologies, with innovations such as cooled CCDs, backside-illuminated CCDs, and antireflective coatings being introduced to enhance quantum the efficiency. These innovations enabled the creation of high quantum-efficiency CCDs, which dramatically improved the sensitivity and accuracy in detecting optical signals. Together with the rapid development of digital imaging in the 1990s, these innovations collectively transformed dark-field microscopy into cutting-edge fields such as nanophotonics, −
nonlinear optics, , and quantum imaging.

sec.p:
Plasmonics, the study of interactions between light and plasmonic materials, encompasses both localized surface plasmon resonances (LSPRs), which arise in metallic nanostructures, and surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs), which can propagate along smooth, unstructured metal–dielectric interfaces. The field of plasmonics has a rich history that began in the fourth century. It was documented in 1857 with Faraday’s synthesis and observation of Au nanocolloids, and later formalized in 1957 when Ritchie introduced the concept of SPPs. This was followed by key advances in the 1970s, −
including the discovery of surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS), which revealed the ability of plasmonic nanostructures to amplify electromagnetic fields. , These theoretical and experimental advances laid the foundation for modern plasmonics. However, the field of plasmonics, particularly at the single-particle level, benefited greatly from the advancements of spectroscopy and high quantum-efficiency CCD technologies. The development of high-resolution spectral analysis, which originated from Fraunhofer’s slit-prism system to NASA’s hyperspectral imaging, along with the development of high quantum-efficiency CCDs, became critical for uncovering the optical properties of nanoscale materials. As interest in nanotechnology surged during the late 20th century, the exploration of nanoscale phenomena spurred the development of advanced imaging techniques. Scanning near-field optical microscopy enabled the observation of single-particle plasmon spectra and near-field images. , In the early 2000s, the advent of single-particle dark-field scattering imaging and spectroscopy techniques allowed scientists to study individual nanoparticles rather than averaging over particle ensembles. , It deepened the fundamental understanding of plasmonic phenomena and accelerated the development of rich applications. Today, dark-field microscopy continues to be an indispensable tool for plasmonics, driving its rapid growth and bridging the gap between nanoscale optical studies and real-world applications.

Dark-field scattering imaging and spectroscopy are powerful optical techniques that enable the visualization and analysis of nanoscale materials and processes with exceptional sensitivity and contrast. They provide critical insights into the optical properties of plasmonic nanoparticles, such as their shapes, −
compositions, −
spectral responses, −
and polarization behaviors. −
One of the most fundamental applications is the acquisition of scattering images and spectra, which are directly tied to the plasmonic properties and scattering cross sections of nanoparticles. −
The optical behaviors of various plasmonic nanoparticles, including nanospheres (NSs), −
nanocubes (NCs), ,−
nanorods (NRs), ,, nanoplates, −
nanorings, , and nanostars, −
have been studied extensively to understand how the size, shape, and composition affect their scattering properties. For example, long Ag NRs exhibit anisotropic scattering patterns owing to their elongated shape (Figure a), where the scattering intensity varies with the orientation of the NR relative to linearly polarized light. This property is particularly useful for analyzing shape anisotropy and understanding how the nanoparticle morphology affects the scattering behavior. ,, Furthermore, this anisotropic scattering behavior can be exploited in color routing, ,, where the directionality of scattered light is leveraged for optical signal modulation and manipulation. When linearly polarized light is used, the scattering intensity depends on the alignment of the electric field vector with the long axis of a nanoparticle, which adds another dimension of analysis for studying the orientation and polarization sensitivity of plasmonic nanoparticles. −
More details on polarization-dependent measurements will be discussed in Section . Dark-field scattering microscopy is also invaluable for monitoring dynamic processes in real time. ,−
For example, the in situ monitoring of Ag@Hg NRs during Hg ion incorporation reveals plasmon peak shifts as the aspect ratio is changed, enabling direct observation of structural transformations (Figure b). Similarly, dark-field scattering microscopy has been employed to track nanoparticle dissolution in corrosive environments, where changes in scattering intensity and color provide evidence of degradation. −
In catalytic reactions, this technique allows surface changes to be monitored as reactants adsorb or desorb on plasmonic catalysts, −
while in colloidal systems, it enables the tracking of aggregation and self-assembly processes. −
Such capabilities also enable the precise tracking of cellular processes in a biomedical context, such as the alteration of the cell morphology with high spatial and temporal resolution. −
For example, dynamic imaging of live cells labeled with antiepidermal growth factor receptor-functionalized nanoparticles reveals color changes corresponding to receptor reorganization during ligand binding and intracellular trafficking (Figure c). In addition, dark-field imaging has been used to monitor drug delivery, with spectral shifts indicating cellular internalization, −
drug release, −
and nanoparticle degradation. ,, This approach has also facilitated the real-time study of receptor-mediated interactions and cellular uptake of plasmonic nanoparticles, −
providing valuable insights for designing precise drug delivery platforms. Beyond biomedical applications, dark-field scattering has become a key tool in the study of light–matter interactions in nanophotonic systems. ,, For instance, nanoparticle-on-mirror structures create ultrasmall mode volumes and enhanced electromagnetic fields, facilitating effects like Rabi splitting (Figure d), −
and quantum tunneling in plasmonic structures. Dark-field microscopy is also uniquely suited for resolving resonant mode distributions, such as whispering gallery modes, and identifying interference-induced nonradiating states, such as anapole modes. ,, From its foundational use in microscopy to its current role in cutting-edge research, dark-field imaging now serves as a cornerstone for investigating nanoscale systems and advancing modern science.

sec.p: At the forefront of advancements in dark-field scattering imaging and spectroscopy lies a rich history shaped by progress in optics, plasmonics, and humanity’s drive to explore the natural world. Once a basic tool for microscopy, the dark-field technique has evolved into sophisticated methods for nanoscale investigations. This tutorial serves as an introductory guide for those who are new to the field, offering a foundation to navigate the principles and applications of dark-field scattering imaging and spectroscopy. We begin by outlining the fundamental principles of dark-field scattering microscopy and detailing the basic experimental setups. From there, we explore its applications at the single-particle level, including widely adopted configurations, polarization-dependent measurements, and circular differential scatterometry. To further expand the capabilities of dark-field scattering microscopy, we introduce k-space imaging and hyperspectral dark-field imaging. We finally discuss the key performance metrics and highlight emerging applications. By bridging the gap between the fundamental principles and innovative applications, we aim to inspire and equip newcomers to contribute to the ongoing evolution of dark-field scattering microscopy and spectroscopy.

sec.title: Fundamentals of Dark-Field Scattering
sec.p: Dark-field scattering microscopy differs from conventional bright-field microscopy, where the background appears bright, and objects are dark. In contrast, the background remains dark because the direct illumination is deliberately blocked from entering the collection path of the objective in dark-field scattering microscopy. As a result, only the light scattered by the target sample is collected, resulting in bright objects on a dark background. This technique is particularly valuable for collecting and analyzing scattered light from nanostructures, making it essential for studying different optical resonances in these systems.

Light scattering typically occurs when light passes through a nonuniform medium with local refractive index differences, causing light propagation to deviate from its original trajectory. Developed by Gustav Mie in 1908, the Mie theory provides an exact analytical solution to describe the optical response of spherical particles based on the dielectric properties of the material and interface boundary conditions. The Mie theory gives the scattering cross-section (C sca) of a spherical particle as follows 1 Csca=2πk2∑n=1∞(2n+1)(|an|2+|bn|2) where k is the wavevector of the incident light; a
n and b
n are the two sets of the most important coefficients that determine the scattering properties of the sphere, and they represent the n th-order electrical and magnetic resonance modes. The scattering of spherical particles can be understood as a superposition of optical radiation arising from dipolar, quadrupolar, and higher-order electric and magnetic resonances. It is affected by the refractive indices of the spherical particle and the surrounding medium, as well as the radius of the sphere. The analytical method of the Mie theory allows one to rapidly calculate the scattering spectra of spherical nanostructures and, importantly, decompose the contributions of different resonance modes in the spectrum. This provides a clear physical image that helps to explain experimental observations. The Mie theory is not limited to homogeneous spheres but can also be extended to analyze the scattering behaviors of layered spherical structures, such as core@shell nanoparticles (e.g., a gold core with a silica shell) or complex core–multishell configurations. −
By adapting the Mie solution to account for multiple concentric layers with distinct refractive indices and thicknesses, the theory provides analytical insights into how the optical properties and geometry of each layer collectively affect the scattering spectra. This capability is particularly valuable for designing multifunctional nanostructures used in applications such as targeted drug delivery, plasmon-enhanced spectroscopy, , and tunable metamaterials. In addition to the Mie theory, various numerical methods developed later can also be used to solve the electromagnetic responses of arbitrarily shaped nanostructures and heterostructures. −
As an exact analytical solution for spherical particles, the Mie theory serves as a critical benchmark for validating numerical simulations. Beginners can compare their simulation results against Mie-derived predictions to verify accuracy, identify meshing errors, and refine boundary conditions. This practice ensures robust modeling before tackling more complex and nonspherical systems. In past decades, resonant light scattering by metal and high-index dielectric nanoparticles has aroused great interest. Because the dielectric properties of metal and dielectric materials are vastly different, the physical origins of resonant light scattering in these two types of nanoparticles differ largely, which can be well understood using the Mie theory. Scattering on metal (e.g., Au and Ag) nanoparticles is attributed to LSPRs, the excitation of the collective oscillations of free electrons. LSPRs endow metal nanoparticles with large absorption and scattering cross sections, enabling strong light–matter interactions. In addition, LSPRs in metal nanoparticles are sensitive to the material composition, nanoparticle size and shape, which allows for synthetic control across a wide spectral range. −
High-index dielectric nanoparticles, such as Si NSs, can also support enhanced light–matter interactions owing to Mie resonances. Mie resonances originate from induced displacement currents inside dielectric nanoparticles. Dielectric nanoparticles have low losses at optical frequencies, which is considered to be complementary to their plasmonic counterparts in various nanophotonic applications.

sec.title: Common System Setups of Dark-Field Scattering Microscopy
sec.p: A dark-field scattering system generally consists of three components: a light source, a microscope with dark-field illumination, and a camera for image capture or dynamic monitoring. Tungsten-halogen lamps with a continuous distribution of light intensity over a wide spectral range (350–2500 nm) are widely employed as the light sources. There are various methods to realize dark-field illumination, primarily by blocking incident and stray light. Figure illustrates three widely used dark-field measurement setups, including the forward scattering configuration, the backward scattering configuration, and the evanescent scattering configuration. The first two configurations share similar principles by using high-angle dark-field excitation geometries, while the last one utilizes evanescent wave illumination.

caption.p: Schematics of the three types of experimental setups for dark-field scattering microscopy. (a) Forward scattering configuration. (b) Backward scattering configuration. (c) Evanescent dark-field scattering. The dashed arrows denote the excitation light that cannot be collected.

sec.p: The key component of the forward scattering configuration is a dark-field condenser placed beneath a transparent substrate, such as a glass slide and an indium tin oxide (ITO) substrate, to direct incident light at a highly oblique angle (Figure a). The incident white light first passes through an opaque stop, transforming into a ring-shaped light beam. It is then deflected by a set of lenses in the condenser, finally illuminating the sample as a hollow light cone. Normal bright- or dark-field objectives can be used for light collection. An important parameter to consider in this configuration is the NA. The NA represents the ability of a lens to collect light, which is defined as 2 NA=nsin⁡θ where n is the refractive index of the medium between the sample and the objective, typically air or oil, and θ is the half angle of the light cone, i.e., the incidence angle of the excitation light. NA takes into account both the refractive index of the imaging medium and the angular aperture of the objective. One should note that the NA value of the condenser must be larger than that of the objective to enable dark-field illumination. There are two main types of condensers depending on the working medium: dry dark-field condensers in air and immersion dark-field condensers with water or oil between the condenser and the slide. Immersion dark-field condensers are preferred for high NA applications, with the upper NA limit reaching 1.50 and a corresponding incidence angle of 83°.

For immersion dark-field condensers, a drop of oil is applied to the front lens, and the condenser should be raised until the oil contacts the bottom surface of the glass slide. Special care should be taken to prevent the formation of bubbles in the oil. After observation, the oil droplet should be carefully removed using lens paper and a suitable cleaning solution. One should also note that the actual NA value can be reduced when tested nanostructures are immersed in an aqueous medium, as the refractive index of water limits the deflection angles of light passing through the glass slide (n = 1.515) into the aqueous solution (n = 1.336). Readers are encouraged to explore online resources provided by microscope manufacturers for more detailed information on microscope components and application techniques. ,

The backward scattering configuration (Figure b) is different from the forward scattering one in two aspects. First, the backward scattering configuration uses reflected light illumination, allowing for the use of nontransparent substrates and offering greater flexibility for material characterization. Second, the “condenser” is integrated coaxially with the objective lens, known as the dark-field objective. In the backward scattering configuration (Figure b), the incident light is typically oriented perpendicular to the optical axis of the microscope. The light first travels through an opaque stop, forming a ring-shaped light beam. The beam is then reflected by a 45° tilted annular silver mirror and passes through the hollow collar surrounding the dark-field objective. A set of circular mirrors or prisms at the bottom of the hollow collar acts as a dark-field condenser to deflect the light beam at highly oblique angles. The dark-field objective is situated in the inner chamber, ensuring that the reflected light from the substrate misses the front lens, allowing only the scattered light to be collected. Figure a and b show the two most representative high-angle dark-field excitation configurations, corresponding to typical commercially available setups. Alternative, more flexible laboratory configurations also exist. −
For example, one flexible approach uses a fiber-coupled white light source positioned beside a microscope to achieve high-angle illumination, while scattered light is collected using a conventional objective with an appropriate NA. This setup eliminates the need for a specialized dark-field condenser or microscope, simplifying implementation and offering enhanced modulation flexibility. Notably, it enables edge illumination with incidence angles up to 90 deg, which is unattainable with the configurations displayed in Figure a,b. However, this method also has limitations. Its directional illumination makes scattering excitation sensitive to nanoparticle orientation, which is problematic for anisotropic structures. In such cases, the measured scattering signal becomes strongly dependent on the orientation of the nanoparticle relative to the incident light. As a result, a single measurement may not capture the overall optical behavior. A comprehensive spectral profile thus requires sample rotation and repeated measurements across multiple orientations, increasing the acquisition time and reducing the time efficiency compared to azimuthally symmetric illumination schemes.

In addition to high-angle excitation methods, evanescent waves are an excellent choice for dark-field illumination owing to their near-field characteristics. The evanescent field decays exponentially and interacts only with materials within a depth comparable to the wavelength of the excitation light. This near-field property makes evanescent scattering microscopy a powerful technique for label-free single-molecule detection and tracking molecular motions at the subnanometer level. Evanescent wave illumination can be achieved by using a glass prism to produce total internal reflection and excite the evanescent wave (Figure c), a method known as total internal reflection microscopy. Additional methods for evanescent wave illumination have also been developed through a dielectric slab waveguide, and SPPs along the surface of a gold film.

Overall, all the three excitation methods have their own advantages and disadvantages (Table ). The forward scattering configuration requires the transmitted light illumination. It is therefore ideal for transparent samples, such as cells and nanoparticles in solution, owing to high contrast from scattered light. However, the transmitted light illumination prohibits the use of opaque samples. The need for precise alignment of the condenser and the objective is another disadvantage of the transmitted excitation method since the misalignment compromises imaging and contrast. The backward scattering configuration using reflective light illumination is versatile for both transparent and opaque materials and requires no alignment but less effective for low-refractive-index materials. Evanescent scattering offers unparalleled surface sensitivity but is restricted to ultrathin regions near interfaces. Also, the penetration depth of evanescent waves depends on the wavelength and incident angle, which might limit the versatility of this method. As a result, the choice of the dark-field excitation configuration depends on the properties of the target sample and experimental goals.

sec.p: The dark-field illumination configurations described above are typically integrated into modern infinity-corrected microscopes, equipped with eyepieces for observation or cameras for imaging. The dark background offers high contrast for imaging nanoparticles much smaller than the diffraction limit and biological samples with refractive indices close to those of their surrounding environments. Recently, artificial intelligence (AI) using deep learning has been introduced in dark-field microscopy. Deep learning algorithms are highly effective in solving complex inverse problems and reconstructing imaging processes with improved speed and resolution. , We believe that AI applications will profoundly advance the capabilities of dark-field microscopy in the near future.

sec.title: Single-Particle Dark-Field Scattering Imaging and Spectroscopy
sec.p: In comparison with ensemble measurements analyzing the average behavior of a population, single-particle measurements allow the optical properties of individual nanoparticles to be studied. These measurements can be combined with numerical simulation methods and advanced three-dimensional (3D) tomography reconstruction techniques to better understand the precise interplay between nanoparticle structures and optical properties. , Single-particle measurements are also able to reveal variations and rare events that get averaged out in ensemble methods. For example, nanoparticle dimers and trimers in different geometrical configurations randomly assembled during sample preparation can be selected and examined with single-particle measurements, paving the way for exploring new plasmonic resonance modes and the resultant light scattering properties. ,, Single-particle measurements also establish an important platform for studying plasmon-mediated interactions down to the single-molecule regime. , Single-particle dark-field scattering measurements are essential for the analysis of the optical resonances of nanoparticles. High-sensitivity spectrometers are required to provide adequate signal-to-noise ratios for individual nanoparticles. Small single particles may not be detected because of weak scattering signals. In this section, we introduce the basic setups for performing single-particle dark-field scattering measurements and approaches for combining polarization-dependent measurements.

sec.title: Basic Setups
sec.p: The basic setup for single-particle dark-field scattering measurements typically consists of a microscope with dark-field illumination, a camera for imaging, and a spectrometer for spectroscopic analysis. Figure a shows the schematic of a typical system. The signal light collected by the objective is split into two beams. One passes through a tube lens for imaging by the camera on the top, and the other is focused onto the spectrometer for spectral measurements. The use of a beam splitter in this configuration inevitably reduces the signal intensity. Alternatively, using a switchable mirror can select the light path for imaging or spectral measurements without sacrificing the signal intensity.

The signal light is divided into two beams and transmitted to the camera for imaging and the spectrometer for spectroscopic analysis, respectively. A dark-field scattering image of an individual Au NS with a diameter of 100 nm is placed next to the camera as an example. (b) Schematic illustrating how the slit is used to selectively capture scattered light from a targeted nanoparticle. (c) Scattering images obtained in the mirror mode, demonstrating single-particle selection achieved by positioning a slit at the spectrometer entrance. (d) Scattering images obtained in the mirror mode (left) and grating mode (right) when multiple nanoparticles are present within the slit. The scattering spectrum of a targeted nanoparticle (white arrow, left panel) is acquired in the grating mode by vertically integrating the signal within a defined region (white dashed box, right panel) at each wavelength.

sec.p: The signal light entering the spectrometer is further focused, recollimated, and directed to either a mirror (for imaging) or a grating (for spectral measurements), eventually reaching a CCD array detector with sufficient resolution and sensitivity for single-particle measurements. The entrance slit of the spectrometer plays a critical role in such measurements. As illustrated in Figure b, scattered light from nanoparticles is deflected and refocused into the spectrometer. The slit effectively blocks scattered light and optical images originating from nontargeted nanoparticles, thereby ensuring that only signals from the region of interest are acquired. In a typical single-particle measurement, a targeted nanoparticle is first centered within the field of view under the operation in the mirror mode (left panel, Figure c). The entrance slit of the spectrometer is then narrowed to exclude signals from other nanoparticles (right panel, Figure c). A narrower slit width enhances spatial selectivity and signal isolation. The system is subsequently switched to the grating mode for spectral measurements. Although multiple nanoparticles may be present within the slit (left panel, Figure d), their spectral measurements are assumed to remain independent as long as their images are well separated spatially (right panel, Figure d). However, nanoparticle clusters or large contaminants with exceptionally strong scattering should be removed from the field of view to prevent the introduction of stray light. The scattering spectrum of the targeted nanoparticle is obtained in the grating mode through the vertical integration of the signal within a predefined region at each wavelength. To accurately extract the scattering spectrum of the targeted nanoparticle, the selected region (white dashed box in the right panel of Figure d) must fully encompass the nanoparticle’s scattering signal in the y-direction without overlapping with the scattering signals from other nanoparticles. This ensures that the spectral integration is performed exclusively on the targeted nanoparticle, free from cross-talk or contamination by adjacent signals.

A dark-field scattering spectrum reveals how much light is scattered at each wavelength for a given excitation light source. One should note that the measured spectrum is not the actual scattering spectrum. Data processing, including background subtraction and light source calibration, is required. The formula used for data processing is 3 S(λ)=[Snp0(λ)−Sbg0(λ)]/L0(λ) where S(λ) is the corrected scattering spectrum, S np0(λ) is the directly measured spectrum from the target nanoparticle, obtained by integrating the scattering intensities at each wavelength from the particle region, S bg0(λ) is the background spectrum extracted from the adjacent clean region, and L 0(λ) represents the spectral profile of the excitation source. The configuration of the light source is kept identical during all measurement procedures. The scattering defined by eq has an arbitrary unit. As specified by eq , the raw scattering spectrum measured from a target nanoparticle is first subtracted by the background spectrum to establish a zero baseline. The resultant signal is then normalized against the spectrum of the excitation source. In the procedure of calculation, the background spectrum acquired from a particle-free region serves as the baseline noise of the detection system. The method for acquiring the excitation spectrum varies depending on the experimental configuration. For instance, in both transmission and reflection setups, the excitation source can be measured directly and used for calibration. However, in an evanescent configuration, it is challenging to precisely define the excitation spectrum incident on the nanoparticle. This difficulty arises because the evanescent field has a penetration depth, which is dependent on the excitation wavelength, the incidence angle of the light beam, and the refractive index of the involved medium. , It is noteworthy that evanescent-wave calibration was performed mostly for fluorescence measurements. , This scenario is simplified by two factors. One is that the sizes of fluorescent molecules are usually much smaller than the penetration depth, and the other is that the use of monochromatic excitation results in a single, well-defined penetration depth approximately equal to the excitation wavelength. In contrast, obtaining a dark-field scattering spectrum requires broadband excitation. Since the penetration depth varies with wavelength and is often comparable to the dimensions of nanoparticles, it is difficult to quantitatively determine the exact excitation spectrum experienced by a nanoparticle. Consequently, evanescent wave-based setups are more frequently employed for dark-field imaging applications. The responses of the optical system components, such as the CCD camera and the objective, are wavelength-sensitive, which means that the measured signal (S 1) is the intrinsic signal (S 0) multiplied by the response coefficient R(λ). The dark-field scattering spectrum measured from an optical system without response calibration can thus be written as 4 S(λ)=[Snp1(λ)−Sbg1(λ)]/[L1(λ)]=[Snp0(λ)−Sbg0(λ)]/L0(λ)

The two equations given above are equivalent, which allows us to disregard the influence of the response of the entire optical system. Therefore, the scattering spectrum is often obtained experimentally through the measurements related to eq . It should be noted that the measured S(λ) is closely related but not identical to the simulated/calculated scattering efficiency/cross-section. On the one hand, many setups only allow scattering to be measured in a limited angular range, which does not reflect the total scattering in all directions, especially when the scattering is angularly dependent. This issue can also be understood within the framework of the Mie theory (eq ). In this formulation, the wavevector magnitude k is used to define the size parameter of a nanoparticle of radius r as x = kr, which in turn determines the resonance conditions, spectral position, and efficiency of scattering. In a practical dark-field microscope, the optical configuration functions as a filter in the wavevector space. Illumination is confined to high-angle propagating waves, thereby excluding specularly reflected or directly transmitted light from the collection cone of the objective. Consequently, the detected signal consists exclusively of light scattered by the nanoparticle into wavevectors falling within the NA of the objective. Thus, the experimental geometry effectively probes a specific subset of the total scattering cross-section described by the Mie theory. In addition, some optical components in the setup are sensitive to the polarization of light, which is not taken into account in the regular calibration. The spectrometer may not cover the full spectral range needed to capture all scattering features, particularly for materials with broad optical resonances. Therefore, there are many complex factors that lead to discrepancies between measured and simulated/calculated scattering. On the other hand, simulations often assume idealized conditions (e.g., perfect spheres and isotropic materials) that may not reflect the actual conditions of the sample. Computational methods can also introduce errors owing to discretization, especially for particles with sharp features or very small dimensions. As a result, the measured scattering spectra often need to be analyzed together with the calculated/simulated results.

Figure illustrates a typical procedure for single-particle scattering characterization with Au NSs as an example. A well-dispersed Au NS sample was observed, and a region of interest was selected for single-particle scattering measurements (Figure a). The region was then identified in scanning electron microscopy (SEM) using a pattern-matching method (Figure b), which will be introduced below. The single-particle spectrum was calculated and correlated with the particle morphology for further analysis (Figure c,d).

sec.p: We would like to highlight some important considerations for conducting single-particle scattering measurements.

sec.title: Remove the Infrared Radiation (IR)-Blocking Component from Halogen Lamps
sec.p: Halogen lamps are commonly used as white light sources for dark-field scattering measurements. These lamps often have IR-blocking components, such as a ground glass diffuser or an IR cutoff filter, at the outlet to block infrared emissions and reduce thermal effects. However, this limits the spectral range below ∼750 nm, which is narrower than the response of most commercial CCD cameras. Removing IR-blocking component is recommended to maximize the active spectral range for measurements.

sec.title: Capture Scattering Images with a CCD Camera Detector
sec.p: The CCD camera detector on the spectrometer can be used to capture scattering images for the analysis of far-field radiation. Using a magnified scattering image reveals more details of the spatial distribution. This can be achieved by properly adjusting the magnification of the lens in front of the spectrometer to take advantage of more pixels on the CCD camera for imaging. In addition, under the grating mode, a spectrally resolved scattering image can be obtained by narrowing the slit of the spectrometer, with the x- and y-axis representing the spectral and spatial distributions of the far-field radiations from the target sample.

sec.title: Pattern-Matching Method
sec.p: Pattern matching is crucial for correlating dark-field scattering data with the morphological structures of nanoparticles. This process can be challenging because the contrast in SEM images is typically much lower than that in scattering images. In addition, the small field of view in SEM observation, particularly under high magnifications, complicates one-to-one matching with nanoparticles in the scattering image. Artificial markers, such as scratches and inkblots, are often necessary to locate target nanoparticles. Easily identifiable contaminants at low magnifications can also be used as markers. It should be noted that surface scratches and random contaminants often generate intense scattering signals, which can obscure the detection of nearby nanoparticles. Maintaining an adequate separation from such features is therefore essential. In contrast, markers with weak scattering, such as those fabricated by microfabrication methods, represent a more suitable alternative. A set of images at different magnifications, including both the markers and the nanoparticles, facilitates retrieving the targeted region in the subsequent characterization. Consistent sample orientation throughout the entire characterization process further aids in pattern matching.

sec.title: Influence of NA and Magnification
sec.p: The NAs and magnifications of objectives and condensers affect both excitation and collection angles. One should select an appropriate NA and magnification according to experimental requirements. For example, an objective with a higher NA is needed for measuring high-angle radiations, such as those from out-of-plane dipole modes. The use of objectives and condensers with high NAs and magnifications generally enhances signal-to-noise ratios, benefiting single-particle measurements.

sec.title: Stray Light from the Environment or Adjacent Particles
sec.p: Stray light from the surrounding environment, such as displays, smart phones, and indoor lighting, or adjacent particles can alter the spectral shape of target objects or introduce stray peaks into scattering spectra. To mitigate this, one should ensure that the light path of the system is properly encapsulated to block ambient light. Conducting measurements in a darkroom can also be beneficial. To minimize stray light from adjacent particles, one is suggested to use a clean substrate and a narrow slit, choose well-dispersed samples, reduce contaminating particles as much as possible, and avoid objects with significant height differences.

sec.title: Differences in the Forward and Backward Scattering Signals
sec.p: Both the forward and backward scattering configurations are commonly used for single-particle measurements (Figure ). However, one should keep in mind that these signals can differ for specific structures, in particular, those with directional scattering capabilities. For example, directional forward scattering occurs when the scattered fields from the electric and magnetic dipole resonances of dielectric nanoparticles interfere destructively in the backward direction. ,

sec.title: Influence of Substrates
sec.p: The scattering spectra of nanoparticles can be affected by the supporting substrate (Figure ). The following guidelines serve as a primer for understanding these effects. Low-refractive-index substrates with smooth surfaces, such as glass slides (n = ∼1.4–1.5), are preferable for revealing the intrinsic scattering characteristics of nanoparticles. ITO substrates are a good choice when both dark-field scattering measurements and SEM characterization are required. However, ITO substrates have a higher refractive index (n = ∼1.9) compared to glass substrates, causing variations in the scattering spectra. When high-refractive-index substrates (n > 2.5) are employed, both the scattering intensity and spectral shape can change significantly owing to the coupling between plasmonic nanoparticles and the substrate. ,,, As a rule of thumb, a substrate of a high refractive index induces a large redshift in the plasmon resonance owing to the increased local dielectric constant. Furthermore, the symmetry breaking introduced by a dielectric substrate can radiatively brighten otherwise dark or out-of-plane modes, ,, making them spectroscopically accessible. Take the widely used silicon substrate as an example. A new peak corresponding to the out-of-plane plasmon mode emerges when a gold NS is deposited (Figure a). For layered structures, thin-film interference effects can act as a spectral filter, either enhancing or suppressing the scattering signal at specific wavelengths. The Si/SiO2 (300 nm thick) substrate, often used to study the coupling between two-dimensional (2D) materials and plasmonic nanoparticles, shows a reflectance valley around 600 nm owing to the thin-film interference effect. Scattering within such a spectral range is suppressed when a Si/SiO2 substrate is used. , Finally, when a nanoparticle is positioned near a metal substrate, image charges are produced in the metal substrate and couple with charges in the nanoparticle. This coupling interaction leads to a significant resonance redshift and a modified radiation pattern, which are highly sensitive to the separation distance. This configuration, often termed a nanoparticle-on-mirror structure, generates an extremely confined and enhanced electromagnetic field within the nanoscale gap. Given the complexity introduced by interfaces, we recommend performing comparative simulations with and without a substrate, as this comparison is essential for gaining a deep understanding of observed plasmonic phenomena.

sec.title: Real-Space Imaging and Directionality
sec.p: The scattering pattern of a single nanoparticle can be related to the radiation directionality in specific cases. Although this is not a fully rigorous measure of directionality, there have been many examples verifying its qualitative validity. For instance, a donut-shaped scattering pattern indicates out-of-plane dipole radiations, while a solid spot is related to the radiations from a horizontally lying dipole. Similarly, elongated and color-resolved scattering patterns of individual Ag NRs intuitively demonstrate the distinct far-field radiations from high-order plasmon resonances with odd and even symmetries in Ag NRs. ,,

sec.title: Polarization-Dependent Dark-Field Scattering
sec.p: Polarization-dependent dark-field scattering spectroscopy emerges as a powerful tool for studying the shape and orientation of individual anisotropic plasmonic nanoparticles by observing their scattering responses to linearly polarized light. This technique aids in distinguishing different plasmon modes of nanoparticles and probing their symmetries. The intricate relationship between the polarization-dependent optical response and the anisotropy of nanoparticles holds promise for applications in orientation sensing and polarization-based encryption. ,,,

The polarization-dependent dark-field scattering microscopy setup typically consists of a butterfly shaped light blocker and a linear polarizer positioned between the incident light and the objective lens. The blocker selectively allows a portion of the incident light, indicated by two white areas in Figure a, to pass through the objective and illuminate the nanoparticles on a substrate at specific azimuth angles. Figure illustrates two primary incident polarization components, which are p- and s-polarization. The blue and red arrows represent the k-vector and the polarization direction of the incident light, respectively. In p-polarized excitation, the polarization aligns parallel to the plane of incidence (xz-plane), whereas for s-polarized light, the polarization is perpendicular to the plane of incidence. The polarization direction of the incident light can be altered between p- and s-polarization by rotating the polarizer by 90° (Figure a,c). The excitation polarization can also be adjusted by rotating the sample. The scattered light of nanoparticles under the excitation of linearly polarized light will then pass through the objective and the circular hole in the center (Figure a,c), and finally be collected by the detector.

sec.p: After the optical setup is properly configured, the next step involves the selection of the polarization and incident directions. To exemplify this process, we utilize the polarization-dependent dark-field measurement on Au NRs as a tutorial example. Au NRs exhibit two significant LSPR modes, longitudinal and transverse resonance modes, with collective electron oscillations occurring along the length and diameter axes of the NR, respectively. When a NR is supported on a substrate, its optical response can be decomposed into three distinct plasmon modes (Figure e): the horizontal longitudinal mode (oscillations parallel to both the substrate and the long axis), the horizontal transverse mode (oscillations parallel to the substrate but perpendicular to the long axis), and the vertical mode (oscillations perpendicular to the substrate). When the NR is supported by a silica substrate, the horizontal longitudinal mode typically exhibits the strongest scattering. The scattering intensities of the horizontal transverse and vertical modes are weak. In contrast, on a silicon substrate, the vertical mode is significantly enhanced owing to the interaction with the high-refractive-index substrate. The optical responses of Au NRs are determined by the specific excitation manner, as shown in the discussion below. ,

sec.title: Excitation of Plasmon Modes
sec.p: We use the excitation of plasmon modes in Au NRs on a silicon substrate as an example to illustrate the correspondence between the excitation scheme and the excited plasmon mode (Figure e). Under s-polarized excitation, the configuration can be categorized as longitudinal s-polarization and transverse s-polarization, depending on the alignment between the incident electric field direction and the long axis of the NR. When the electric field is parallel to the long axis, the excitation is defined as longitudinal s-polarization; when it is perpendicular to the long axis (while remaining in the substrate plane), it is defined as transverse s-polarization. These two excitation schemes selectively excite the horizontal longitudinal and horizontal transverse modes, respectively. Under p-polarized excitation, the incident electric field can be orthogonally decomposed into the horizontal and vertical components. Figure f displays the measured scattering spectra of a single Au NR on a silicon substrate under three excitation polarization schemes: longitudinal s-polarization, transverse s-polarization, and p-polarization. The longitudinal s-polarization excitation is used to excite the horizontal longitudinal components, which generate two distinct scattering peaks at 540 and 870 nm. In contrast, the transverse s-polarization yields only a single, much weaker and broader resonance. The p-polarized excitation is composed predominantly of the horizontal longitudinal and vertical components owing to the negligible contribution from the weak horizontal transverse mode. The plasmon resonances exhibited by nanoparticles are typically significantly smaller in spatial size compared to the incident light wavelength and can be approximated as polarizable electric point dipoles. When the excitation polarization is aligned parallel to the length axis of the NR, the horizontally oriented radiation torus (in-plane dipole) will be detected by the objective as a solid bright spot. When the excitation polarization is aligned perpendicular to the substrate, the vertically oriented radiation torus (out-of-plane dipole) will be detected by the objective as a doughnut-shaped pattern. The detected far-field scattering pattern under p-polarization excitation will be determined by the relative magnitudes of the net in-plane and out-of-plane electric point dipoles.

sec.title: Polarization Anisotropy
sec.p: The s-polarization excitation can be used for investigating polarization anisotropy. One can rotate the NR and collect the scattering spectra of the NR with different orientations under s-polarization excitation to determine the length axis of the NR. The longitudinal plasmon resonance of the NR can be effectively excited by the longitudinal s-polarization, while the transverse plasmon resonance shows a weak response. In other words, the scattering spectrum with the strongest intensity is obtained when the length axis of the NR is aligned with the linear polarization direction. The polarization anisotropy of an anisotropic nanoparticle can be calculated by polarization anisotropy = (I L – I S)/(I L + I S), where I L and I S denote the scattering intensity of the nanoparticle under the excitation of incident light polarized parallel to the long and short axis of the nanoparticle, respectively. The polarization anisotropy can also be observed through the rotation of the light blocker by 90° to adjust the azimuth angle of the incident linearly polarized light while keeping the direction of the incident polarization and the orientation of the nanoparticle fixed. It is essential to ensure that the incident light intensity is uniform across all angles before conducting the measurements.

sec.title: Circular Differential Scatterometry
sec.p: Scattering circular dichroism (CD) is a powerful spectroscopic technique for probing the chiroptical responses of individual nanostructures. Chiral nanostructures, which cannot be superimposed on their mirror images, exhibit unique interactions with left- and right-handed circularly polarized light (LCP and RCP light). The chiroptical response can be categorized into intrinsic chirality and extrinsic chirality because the chiroptical response is affected by both the geometry of a nanostructure and the direction of incident light. , The intrinsic chiralities of such structures arise from their geometrical chiralities. Extrinsic chirality arises from the chiral interaction between obliquely incident light and anisotropic nanostructures, even when the nanostructure itself is achiral. This phenomenon is commonly referred to as pseudochirality.

Scattering CD measurements involve the use of circularly polarized white light to measure the scattering spectra under LCP and RCP light. The study of chiral plasmonic nanostructures using dark-field microscopy is driven by their promising applications in ultrasensitive chiral sensing and enantioselective processes. Dark-field scattering microscopy can track plasmon-induced chirality transfer from circularly polarized light to achiral nanostructures. This capability establishes it not only as a pathway for designing chiral sensors, but also as a versatile platform for chiral catalysis. Moreover, chiral sensing by dark-field scattering microscopy can be performed down to the single-molecule level, which holds considerable potential for biomedical advances. This approach is promising for enabling the discrimination of enantiomers and offering insights into the chiral origins of biological systems. In scattering CD measurements, unpolarized white light passes through a polarizer set comprised of a linear polarizer and a quarter-wave plate before entering the objective. The polarization direction of the incident light can be altered between LCP and RCP by rotating the quarter-wave plate (Figure a). The polarization handedness convention used in this tutorial is such that the RCP and LCP vectors rotate clockwise and counterclockwise along the propagation axis, respectively. Before data collection, the circular polarization state and the degree of circular polarization of the incident light generated by a proper unpolarized white light source and the first polarizer set at appropriate working wavelengths should be evaluated.

sec.title: Selection of Operation Wavelengths
sec.p: When the operation wavelengths for the white light source and the polarizer set are selected, it is crucial to consider the peak wavelength and peak width of the major scattering CD bands of chiral nanoparticles. Ideally, the working wavelengths of these optical components should cover the wavelength range of the scattering CD bands. While the spectral range of the extinction CD band provides a valuable reference for the selection, the wavelength shift of the scattering CD band resulting from changes in the dielectric environment, such as transitioning from water to air and interaction with the substrate, should be considered.

sec.title: Evaluation of the Incident Circular Polarization
sec.p: The state and degree of circular polarization of the incident light should be carefully examined. A set of detection procedures is needed to determine whether the incident light is circularly polarized and its handedness. The detection is based on the principle that a circularly polarized light will be converted to linear polarization after passing through a quarter-wave plate. The linearly polarized light generated from LCP and RCP light forms an angle of – 45° and +45° relative to the fast axis of the quarter-wave plate, respectively. During the detection process, the incident light to be detected is directed through a quarter-wave plate, a linear polarizer, and collected by a photodetector. Whether the outgoing light from the quarter-wave plate is linearly polarized can be determined by rotating the linear polarizer and reading out the output intensity of the photodetector.

The excitation light employed in actual experiments is usually not perfectly circularly polarized. When the generated circularly polarized light is employed in the upward or backward scattering configuration (Figure a,b), the white light passes through a condenser or an objective before reaching the focal plane. The polarization state of the incident circularly polarized light can be affected by the reflection at the mirror inside the condenser or the objective, converting the ideal circular polarization into elliptical polarization. This effect becomes increasingly pronounced at a higher incidence angle with a large NA. The tight focusing of the condenser results in a high polarization component on the propagation direction. This creates spatially nonuniform polarization states at the focal plane, where the intended circularly polarized incident field degenerates into a nonuniform and complicated polarization field. The polarizer set for generating circularly polarized incidence should be adjusted, and the associated degree of circular polarization should be recorded. A linear polarizer and photodetector are often employed in this case. The intensity of a circularly polarized light in each polarization direction is measured by rotating the linear polarizer. The degree of circular polarization is defined as I min/I max, where I max and I min represent the maximal and minimal intensities, respectively. A correction procedure to account for imperfect circular polarization of the excitation light is required.

A modified CD spectroscopy configuration has recently been reported to circumvent the limitations imposed by high-NA condenser-induced polarization distortions as discussed above. In the optimized setup, the quarter-wave plate and the linear polarizer are positioned in the detection optical path rather than illumination. The fast axis of the quarter-wave plate is oriented at a ± 45° angle relative to the linear polarizer to obtain the LCP and RCP components of the scattering light, respectively, under the illumination of unpolarized white light. Such a chiral scattering measurement will therefore not be affected by the mirror in the dark-field condenser.

sec.title: Stability and Uniformity of the Light Source
sec.p: Ensuring uniform incident light is essential because nonuniform light intensity can lead to heterogeneous excitation of chiral nanoparticles, thereby introducing extrinsic chirality. Multiple measurements are necessary to ensure stable light intensity during measurements. Adjustments should be made to the setup to minimize potential artifacts resulting from fluctuations in light intensity across the sample and the duration of the measurements.

Data collection and processing in scattering CD measurements are similar to those of conventional scattering measurements. Scattering spectra from individual nanoparticles under the excitation of LCP and RCP light are first acquired. The scattering spectra are then corrected by subtracting the background spectra acquired from an adjacent clean region. The corrected scattering spectra under LCP and RCP incident light are finally normalized with the calibrated response spectra of the entire optical system under LCP and RCP incident light, respectively. Scattering CD measurements on achiral plasmonic nanoparticles, such as Au NSs and Au NRs, are helpful in troubleshooting any external factors that can potentially cause chiroptical responses.

The scattering CD measurements on D-handed chiral Au NCs are provided as an example (Figure b). The chiral scattering spectra of Au NRs (Figure c) are first acquired, showing minimal differences in the scattering intensity under LCP and RCP excitation. Such results suggest that our system is feasible for measuring the scattering CD responses of chiral nanoparticles. Distinct differences are seen in the chiral scattering spectra of a single D-handed chiral Au NC under LCP and RCP excitation (Figure d). The scattering g-factor defined as g = 2 × (S LCP – S RCP)/(S LCP + S RCP) is further used to show the scattering chirality, with S LCP and S RCP representing the scattering spectra under LCP and RCP light, respectively. The calculated scattering g-factor spectrum of the chiral Au NC is shown in Figure e. Large variations in the scattering g-factor can be observed among different chiral nanoparticles because of subtle morphological differences of nanoparticles prepared by colloidal chemical synthesis. Several tens of individual nanoparticles are usually measured for a given chiral nanoparticle sample, and the average g-factor spectrum is obtained. In addition, single-particle scattering g-factors can be correlated with the SEM images of individual nanoparticles for deeper understanding of chirality origins.

sec.title: Substrate Effect
sec.p: The supporting substrate can affect the scattering CD response. Our previous work showed that peak shifts can be induced if a substrate with a positive real part of the dielectric constant is used. More interestingly, the inversion of chiroptical responses was observed when the real part of the dielectric constant of the substrate is negative, as observed in the case of chiral Au NCs on Au substrates.

sec.title: More Functions To Enrich Dark-Field Characterization
sec.p: Commonly used dark-field scattering microscopy and spectroscopy setups can be adapted or upgraded with additional functions for diverse applications. We introduce here k-space imaging and dark-field hyperspectral imaging, which complement conventional microscopic characterization.

sec.title: Imaging in the k-Space
sec.p: Imaging in the k-space, also known as Fourier back focal-plane imaging, is based on the Fourier transform principle and collects the information from the back focal plane of the objective for analysis. This technique displays the wavevector distribution of the light beam from the object plane and is widely used to characterize the directional scattering of optical nanoantennas, the emission directionality of nanoemitters, and the orientation of single molecules.

The back focal plane of an objective lens is located inside the objective barrel, making direct imaging challenging. A Bertrand lens is typically used, as it is able to perform the Fourier transform without changing the position of the conjugate plane. Imaging in the k-space in an infinity optical microscope generally includes three basic components: an objective, a tube lens, and a Bertrand lens. Various configurations for k-space imaging exist, depending on the position of the Bertrand lens. For example, the Bertrand lens can be placed either before or after the image plane. Extra relay optical path can be adapted to move the image plane further from the microscope exit port, allowing more flexibility for adding optical elements and image detection.

Figure a gives a typical k-space imaging configuration where the Bertrand lens is inserted into the “infinity” space between the objective and the tube lens. In this setup, the Bertrand lens directly focuses on the back focal plane of the objective, acting as a tube lens. The advantage of this configuration is that aberrations and tolerancing errors are well controlled since the Bertrand lens forms an infinite conjugate pair with the tube lens rather than a finite one, as seen in other configurations. In addition, positioning the Bertrand lens in an infinity space aids in the alignment of optical elements, thus enhancing the observation of sharp features in the Fourier image. We use experimental data to intuitively demonstrate k-space imaging. Figure b–d show various types of nanoparticles on glass and Si substrates, including Au NSs on a glass substrate (Au NS–glass), Au NSs on a Si substrate (Au NS–Si), and Ag NRs on a Si substrate (Ag NR–Si). The in-plane and out-of-plane plasmon modes of these structures allow the observation of different scattering patterns. The Au NS–glass structure under oblique excitation exhibits spatial homogeneous radiation, giving rise to a uniform contrast in its back focal plane image (bottom right panel, Figure b). In contrast, the out-of-plane plasmon modes appear with a high-refractive-index substrate, such as Si, forming a doughnut-shaped scattering pattern. This is evident in the brightness contrast in the back focal plane image. Take the Au NS–Si structure as an example. The in-plane and out-of-plane modes occur at two different wavelengths. The corresponding back focal plane image shows both color and brightness contrast (bottom right panel, Figure c). The brightness contrast is more pronounced in the back focal plane image of the Ag NR–Si structure, where the area near the edge is brighter, demonstrating the double-lobe scattering (bottom right panel, Figure d).

sec.p: A recent study has successfully demonstrated the angle-resolved scattering properties of individual chiral nanoparticles through the k-space imaging methodology. The chiral nanoparticles were illuminated by a collimated white light from a supercontinuum circularly polarized laser. The polarization of the scattering light was analyzed by inserting a quarter-wave plate and a linear polarizer into the collimated portion of the detection optical path between the tube lens and the camera. The k-space mapping through the polarization analyzer enabled the reconstruction of the Stokes parameters. The maps of the Stokes parameters (S 0 and S 3) were obtained under the LCP and RCP excitations, respectively. The measurement of the Stokes parameters is fundamentally important as it enables complete quantification of the polarization properties of the scattered light, thereby yielding insights into polarization-dependent light–matter interactions.

sec.title: Hyperspectral Dark-Field Scattering
sec.p: Hyperspectral imaging integrates traditional microscopy and spectroscopy, capturing both spatial and spectral information simultaneously. The data generated in hyperspectral imaging, known as a hypercube, includes two spatial dimensions (x, y) and one spectral dimension (z). Hyperspectral imaging offers high-throughput measurements and is particularly effective for characterizing the collective behaviors of nanoparticles. It shows promise in areas such as environmental nanotoxicology studies, biomaterial detection, and surgical guidance.

There are four primary strategies for hypercube acquisition: point scanning, line scanning, wavelength scanning, and snapshot imaging. ,, The point scanning approach, also known as whiskbroom imaging, collects spectral data by scanning the sample point-by-point. The method achieves high spatial and spectral resolutions, however, with a low speed. Line scanning, or push-broom imaging, detects one line at a time, offering faster data acquisition. Both whiskbroom and push-broom imaging require an automatic displacement stage. In contrast, wavelength scanning and snapshot imaging allow the camera and sample to remain stationary. Wavelength scanning captures the entire sample at one wavelength at a time using a two-dimensional detector array, progressing through the spectral wavelengths sequentially. Snapshot hyperspectral imaging employs an array of prisms to optically encode the 3D spectral information onto a 2D detector, making it applicable in time-critical scenarios. Moreover, optimization-based algorithms have been developed to reconstruct 3D data cubes with high temporal resolution, expanding 3D hyperspectral imaging into four-dimensional hyperspectral videos. Deep learning methods also show promise in enhancing both the reconstruction quality and speed. , These imaging strategies are realized using hyperspectral spectrometers, combined with specialized processing software and hardware to deal with large data volumes. Similar to single-particle scattering measurements, data processing in hyperspectral dark-field imaging should take into account background subtraction and light source calibration.

sec.title: Concluding Remarks
sec.p: Dark-field scattering microscopy and spectroscopy have been demonstrated as an effective and universal technique for optical measurements of areas with spatial refractive index variations. A key feature of this technique is its ability to efficiently block background noise, enabling high signal-to-noise ratios. It is particularly well-suited for the characterization of plasmonic nanoparticles with large scattering cross sections. We highlight in this tutorial the fundamental principles, structures, and applications of dark-field scattering measurements for plasmonic nanoparticles, focusing on the characterization capabilities based on existing studies. The detection sensitivity and spatial resolution are the primary concerns. The detection sensitivity refers to the ability to read out the signal of the object from background noise. The scattering intensity of a plasmonic nanoparticle scales with the particle radius as R 6. It is therefore very important to determine the smallest detectable nanoparticle size using dark-field scattering measurements. Studies have indicated that the detection limit can be pushed down to 10–20 nm in size as demonstrated with single Au nanoparticles in a liquid environment when the detector sensitivity, excitation power, light collection capability, and background suppression are optimized. , Time-resolved measurements, linked to the detection sensitivity, are achieved by increasing the excitation power and obtaining high-contrast dark-field images at very short exposure time durations. It is important to carefully manage heat dissipation to avoid sample damage. A fast-response camera is highly desirable for time-resolved measurements, which enable single-particle tracking with ∼1 nm spatial precision and 10 μs temporal resolution. The spatial resolution is another important factor. It represents the ability to distinguish individual nanoparticles from adjacent ones. The spatial resolution of optical measurements is limited by the Rayleigh criterion, with modern microscopes achieving spatial resolutions of ∼200 nm.

Plasmonic nanoparticles significantly enhance microscopic and spectroscopic techniques. They act as image contrast agents for scattering-based optical measurements, and provide strong localized field enhancement that facilitates surface-enhanced spectroscopic techniques. Notable examples include SERS and surface-enhanced fluorescence. The emergence of 2D materials has expanded possibilities for detecting light–matter interactions at the quantum level. Single-particle microscopy and spectroscopy are popular approaches for the investigation of plasmon–exciton interactions in these systems. Chiral plasmonic nanoparticles have recently aroused intense interest, with extensive research devoted to local chiral fields and chiral control of nanoemitters. One should be aware of extrinsic chiral signals originating from tilted illumination in dark-field measurements.

Driven by advances in plasmonics, the field of dark-field scattering microscopy and spectroscopy is evolving from a primarily observational tool into an advanced and integrated analytical platform. Several promising directions are emerging. Dark-field scattering methods are increasingly being combined with super-resolution imaging, , which enables direct correlation of nanoscale structures, dynamic processes, and functions. The rapid development of AI is set to play a transformative role. AI-powered systems will facilitate real-time image analysis and spectral interpretation, , paving the way for high-throughput, automated single-particle analysis that enables rapid classification and extraction of physical parameters. Furthermore, the integration of advanced nanophotonic designs with AI is expected to bring significant improvements in both the spatial and spectral resolution of dark-field techniques. Instrumentation is also poised for major progress. The development of miniaturized spectrometers and integrated photonic devices , is likely to make dark-field scattering setups more compact and portable. This will lead to robust, user-friendly instruments that can be widely adopted by nonspecialists across diverse fields, thereby broadening the range of application scenarios.

Despite this promising trajectory, the transition from qualitative to quantitative spectroscopy remains a fundamental challenge. This difficulty stems from two primary factors. First, the reproducible synthesis of nanoparticles with atomic-level precision and the creation of perfectly controlled, well-characterized substrates remain technically demanding. Second, the measured scattering signal is highly susceptible to a complex interplay of multivariate factors, including the intrinsic material properties of a nanoparticle, its precise geometry, and the influence of the multilayer substrate environment. Consequently, these inherent variabilities pose a significant challenge to the achievement of reproducibility and standardization across experiments.

Overall, we believe that ongoing research studies in plasmonics and advancements in dark-field scattering, microscopic, and spectroscopic technologies are expected to mutually promote each other, pushing forward the forefront of nanophotonics and nanoscience.
